speakeroldname: Mr. Francis G. LeBlanc (Cape Breton Highlands- Canso):
subtopic: FORGIVENESS OF DEBTS (SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA) ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It is a pleasure to speak on this very important topic and to address this issue of assistance to developing countries, particularly in sub-Saharan Africa. As we all know, one of the most important issues of our time has been the growing burden of debt in the Third World. You are probably familiar with the old adage, Mr. Speaker, which states that "if I owe $1 million I have a problem. If I owe $100 million, the bank has a problem. But if I owe $1 billion, everybody has a problem". The situation with respect to world debt is just that. It is a problem not only for the countries involved, but a problem for all of us here in Canada and around the world.
While we support the general thrust of this legislation, we believe the government could go further in showing compassion and leadership in resolving this situation affecting the poorest of our developing nations. It is time for the government to demonstrate that Canada has a role to play in relieving the problems of the developing world, particularly those in Africa where we have had such a history of assistance under previous Liberal governments.
The recent cuts in CIDA funding which were announced in the budget do not augur well for the status that Canada has in the developing world. If we are to demonstrate that leadership role then we must continue to extend ourselves beyond what is reasonable to show our generosity to the Third World.
I must say it is more than just being generous, it is also good economics. Let us face it, many of these countries will never be able to pay their debts, and our forgiveness of the debts of these countries is really an accommodation to reality. Now, as the 20th century closes, we have entirely new challenges on the horizon on a world scale, in particular the dramatic problems of the environment, the question of the greenhouse effect and the depletion of our forests and our natural resources particularly in the Third World.
In North America and developed countries we have belatedly realized, after a century or two of profligacy, that we have depleted the forests. Suddenly we are asking the developing world to recognize that the destruction of their forests and the deforestation of their lands and their agricultural practices in the past are slowly strangling this planet. How can we now impose upon them these additional requirements, along with the debt that they have acquired in simply trying to feed their peoples, and to keep their economies going in relationship to the demands which the industrial society places on all the world? How can we expect these countries to pay off these accumulated debts and also meet these new challenges which will require major structural changes in their economies and will require attitudes that they have not had the chance to develop.

October 6, 1989
Government Orders
It is a simple case of not only reasonable charity but it is a case of accepting the facts in a situation where these countries have enormous debts which they cannot conceivably pay off.
We have to face facts. This government has to face facts. We have to find ways of accommodating the reality that these countries face. I think Bill C-10 is a small step in the right direction. It will alleviate the debts to us that have been acquired by a number of African countries. Let me list some of them for the record. There is the Republic of Cameroon with which Canada has enjoyed good relationships over the years. By virtue of the its bilingual character and its federation form of government, we have forged many links with Cameroon. It is only fair that we should begin to extend the hand of friendship to this country.
Others are the Republic of the Congo, the Republic of the Ivory Coast, the Gabonese Republic, the Republic of Ghana, the Republic of Kenya, the Democratic Republic of Madagascar and the Republic of Nigeria, the Republic of Senegal, the Kingdom of Swaziland, the Republic of Zaire, the Republic of Zambia, the Republic of Zimbabwe. All these countries in Africa will need assistance from Canada in the future in order to bring their economies into some kind of order and to begin the long process of creating the foundations for prosperity that can be generated through these people.
We should not expect this to occur overnight. The societies in those countries are very different from our own. I can remember as a young student travelling to Africa, spending three months in Zambia and seeing that particular country struggle with trying to meet the demands of its people when it was dependent on one commodity, namely, copper. It had no links with the sea for all of its exports. It depended on rail links to the east and to the west, through Mozambique which was a colony of the Portuguese, and Angola to the west which was also a colony of the Portuguese at the time, or through what was then Rhodesia to South Africa. Zambia is entirely surrounded. It participated in the struggle, which we supported, in order to bring independence to what is now Zimbabwe.
It paid a heavy price for that long struggle which is not over yet. Of course, it accumulated debt, because as the price of copper fluctuated over the last 20 years in response to changes in world demand, which were not of Zambia's making, Zambia's economy had to absorb the
shock and acquire the debt. Changes in demands in countries like Canada, the United States and Europe resulted in changes in the demand for this particular commodity. In order for Zambia to rely less on one commodity and to broaden the structure of its economy, it will require a long and difficult process of industrialization. This is a struggle which all African countries, not only Zambia, have to deal with.
At the same time there are pressures for democratization. There are pressures through contacts with countries like Canada for expanding human rights in those countries. We must take a leadership role in those areas as well. We must also realize that the societies are very different, that the pressures which they face are very different from the pressures that we faced when we were proceeding with our own industrialization many years ago.
My experience in Zambia gave me a concrete example of what those African countries, whose problems will be partially alleviated by this bill, have faced and will continue to face in the years ahead. The United Nations has been focusing on the particular problems of Africa. The problem of hunger is nowhere more severe than in the economies of Africa where the climate and where the political turmoil over the last 35 years through the process of decolonization. It has left the whole continent in a state of upheaval and has created wars, famines, droughts and numerous other problems which are far beyond the capacity of the people of those countries to meet.
I notice that the member for Rosedale is here today. He is well aware, through his experience in Ethiopia, of the situation with the famine that occurred there. I want to compliment him on the role that he played when he was Ambassador to Ethiopia. I am sure he can speak with rich personal experience of the obligation which we have as Canadians in meeting the unfortunate situation which continues to exist in Africa and in supporting the people of these countries in their struggle to improve their lot.
We must not think of this modest piece of debt relief which the government is providing to several countries in Africa as the end. It really is only a small beginning toward extending a hand and participating in the rehabilitation of these countries and allowing them to be full partners with us as we enter into the 21st century.
October 6, 1989

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for bringing to the attention of this House some very important principles and some very important economic directions that this government should be following.
It has been, as he has noted, the tradition of governments of this country to assist those nations which are less developed than our own to achieve an economic development that will be self-sustaining, competitive and, as the hon. member has pointed out, to the advantage of all those industrialized and economically advanced nations.
He did mention one point that I think should be drawn to the attention to this House. That is, in the forgiving of these debts to sub-Saharan nations, we are not so much engaging in a charitable action, but doing something that is economically sound and also very good for our own nation and for western economies as well.
Will the hon. member direct his attention to the concern that some others have raised in other committees that many of these debts, while it appears that we are being generous, are really figments of an imagination inasmuch as they can no longer be paid off and inasmuch as the nations that have these debts are not in a position to satisfy the initial obligation?
By forgiving these debts and the payments thereof, we are not only helping their economy we, at least, are not raising the expectations of our own. Are we not directing our energies in a way that might be a little bit more productive thereby satisfying both a human need as well as an industrial and economic one.

It is true that forgiving the debt is not an act of charity that goes against economic reasoning, but really a recognition of reality. We should not forget that the debts which many of these countries accumulated over the years is partly due to the expectations which were created in industrial countries like our own. We were quite free to lend money to these countries in order that they could buy our products and create a demand for our goods, of what to them are the luxuries of western society, the lure of western society which we, as industrial countries, have encouraged them over the years to pursue. recognition of our own involvement in the affair. Another aspect is that it is pretty hard for an individual to operate under the burden of a debt which he or she cannot conceivably begin to repay.
In a developing country, such as those in Africa, before its citizens can begin to deal with their daily and current requirements they must meet the imposed burden, this obligation, which has been imposed upon them from a previous generation or from outside.
The forgiveness of the debt merely allows these countries to start clearing the slate, to focus on current realities, and if we assist these countries in economic management which is realistic and which enables them to develop consistently and appropriately to their own circumstances, we will not restart this problem to which we, in part, have contributed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this bill. I can only echo the words of the member who just spoke.
This bill, which is the forgiveness of debt for the sub-Saharan countries in Africa, is only a small step in the right direction as far as the alleviation of the debt burden on Third World countries is concerned. This action on the part of Canada is not going to cost the Government of Canada a penny. It has no real impact upon the tax collection. Much of the debt has been in place for a considerable length of time and was considered a soft debt when it was loaned in the first place. It has been gathering interest on our books and has been a controversial subject in the public accounts of Canada because it shows there as an asset which we never have expected to collect. It will not entail any appropriation on the part of the Canadian Parliament. It is a small step, with very little impact as far as Canada is concerned. It is money we loaned that we really never expected to get back.
Third World development and the survival of people in the Third World is a continuing problem. Servicing the debt, which I am almost tempted to say was imposed on many Third World countries, is the most debilitating of all on the development action of the Third World countries. It is very difficult, in fact in many cases impossible, for the Third World country to attempt to service the debt and move in the direction of a sustainable economy.

Government Orders
This bill forgives some of those debts, but the government has not continued in the direction of official development assistance. Instead of increasing the assistance it is giving to Third World countries, this government has reduced that assistance. This is what we all call talking out of both sides of our mouths.
The government, in its rhetoric, has been saying that it will do all these great things to help development in Third World countries of the world, but in actual fact it is cutting development funds.
The cuts in official development assistance mean that we are giving less aid to the debt strapped countries of Central Africa. We are giving less aid even as we suggest that we will no longer try to collect the debt. The forgiveness of these debts does not come anywhere near making up for the effect of cuts in assistance to these countries.
These cuts impact, as usual, on the people who can least afford them. The cut in ODA impacts on the people who have no political clout in most cases. They have no voice in the affairs of the world and are the most vulnerable to reductions in assistance. This runs almost directly counter to the Prime Minister's statement to the United Nations in September 1988, when he stated that Canada has reviewed its official development and the government would increase the quality and quantity of the help we will give.
Almost immediately after that the government proceeded with cuts in ODA. In front of the whole world the Prime Minister recommitted Canada to achieving an ODA of .7 per cent of the GNP by the year 2000, and then he immediately reversed his decision and reduced the amount of assistance we give. Obviously the government's rhetoric is just window dressing.
Our commitment of .7 per cent of the GNP by the year 2000 was pushed back by this government when it first came to power. It is unlikely, unless there is a real turnaround in the policy of the government, that we will even reach that goal. If the indications of the last five years of the Conservative government in Canada are correct, we may be lucky to reach this goal by the year 2040 instead of the year 2000. This means we are not trying to assist a large portion of the population of the world. We should be doing more about it.
Canada is in a unique situation. We are a member of the Commonwealth; we are a member of La Francopho-nie. We are well respected in the United States. We are part of the Group of 7 of industrialized nations of the world and a member now of the Security Council of the United Nations. These roles afford Canada an opportunity to make real differences on the international stage, but if we just speak and do not act, if our rhetoric is not followed up by action, we will quickly be recognized as being all mouth and no action.
The lofty statements made by the Prime Minister have not been followed by the action of the government in the last few years. It is not as if this were good for us because cutting aid jeopardizes Canada's long-term interests. It jeopardizes our interests in trade with the developing world. It jeopardizes our standing and our impact on the developing world in many ways other than economic.
For a short-term gain we are giving away a considerable amount of the impact that we could have had. This is a serious miscalculation on the part of Canada. We claim to be a generous nation, but we stand behind the Scandinavian countries, Holland, Belgium and France, and we are gradually working our way downward in the list of those countries that have been the most generous to the developing world. We are part of the western industrialized countries that seem to spend our time and efforts making sure that instead of allowing these countries to develop, by imposing and insisting on payment of debt-and this is why I say this bill is going in the right direction-we are moving toward making it impossible for Third World countries to grow, develop and become more self-sufficient.
Loans with the kind of interest that is being charged- and again we are working in the direction of reducing the interest on many of the loans-are very detrimental to the survival and the development of Third World countries. We do not have to go far to see the impact of loans that are impossible to pay.
Right now in western Canada in the farm communities there are thousands of farmers who have loans higher than they can possibly service and consequently are in exactly the same position as these Third World countries. If they continue to try to service them, they get further into debt. If they do not continue to service them, they lose their land. Luckily the Third World countries are not likely to be foreclosed on, but the impact of these foreign debts is so long term and so debilitating that it can have the same kind of effect that it does in the local situation of a farmer.
October 6, 1989

We in Canada are supporting the IMF World Bank position on all of these debts. The IMF has been suggesting to countries such as Venezuela, Mexico and the Philippines, you can name dozens of them, and the Third World countries about which we are talking about today, that they must do something about how their economies work. They must restructure their economies so that they can pay this debt, restructure the economies in such a way that the payment of the debt goes before services to the population, the health of the population, even the feeding of the population.
The people in the Philippines tell us that they cannot possibly pay the debt and grow economically. In fact, the imposed structure which requires higher taxes is keeping out investment in the Philippines because there is no way that people will invest in the Philippines as long as the taxes are high in order to pay these debts.
I am going to spend the last few moments on exactly what we should be doing regarding world debt. The only just resolution for the debt crisis in the world is the cancellation of the debt and the allowing of economies to become self-reliant. That way all countries of the world will benefit, the countries that are presently in debt and those countries that trade with them and work with them, because as so go these countries, so goes the world.
Partial debt relief is just not going to work. Even if you forgive half the debt today and leave the other half in place, under the world financial structure, within a few years the debt will be back up to the same size again and be just as debilitating as it was before. In the mean time all of the development funds in that countiy will have gone to alleviate the debt. Every one of these debts has been paid for at least once and some of them twice in interest paid to the countries that have lent the money in some cases. Some of them are not interest bearing for 50 years, but in those cases we did not expect to get the money back anyway.
Government Orders
In 1988 the IMF World Bank made a statement. Again, the World Bank and the IMF are great on declarations but very small on follow-up. They suggested back in 1988 that they recognized the need for the elimination of debt as quickly as possible. Then they turned around and immediately imposed restructuring, which made sure that there would be no development, on a number of countries that are so wallowing in debt that they are almost at the point of not surviving.
The World Council of Churches also made some comments about the direction that the world should go in alleviating the debt problem. It said:
The only way a country can both avoid being restructured from the outside and achieve a responsible-in the sense of first and participatory-development dynamic-Self-reliance-is based on effective control by the people over their country's natural resources and production. Its central productive focus is not response to the external demand, but identifying and acting on internal potentialities to fulfil the peoples' most urgent needs.
That is a very direct quotation which says that what we need to do is to allow these countries to use all of their potential on development. The only way they can do that is if we cancel the debts, all the debts, against Third World countries and give them a chance to become full participants in the economy of the world.
Bill C-10 is a small step toward a solution that could, if it were carried on and if it became the policy of all of the industrial countries of the west, solve the problem. If we do not do it, all that is happening is an action, a little bit of show, which will not change the situation for the struggling people of the world and their attempts to survive.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill does give Canadians and Parliament an opportunity to address what in many ways is perhaps one of the two most important issues on the globe's agenda today. The other is of course the issue of the environment.
Both issues are connected; that is, the issue of the imbalance in economic opportunities and economic development between the rich nations and the poor nations of the world. This bill does confirm a particular step that Canada is taking, but it opens up an opportunity for us to consider in a broader way what Canada is doing in the area of international development.

October 6, 1989
Government Orders
We can no longer afford to see the globe divided into nations and to look at our society as isolated from the world abroad. What is happening in sub-Sahara Africa is happening in our own neighbourhood and we must see that section of the globe as part of our own neighbourhood. A child who dies from hunger in the refugee camps in Malawi must be seen as much as our neighbour as a child who dies from an automobile accident on the Malahat on Vancouver Island. We have to be prepared to devote our community resources to make radical changes in how the world distributes its wealth and in how we look after the people who are part of our human family.
What is the record of the government? It proposes a bill of this kind, but let us look behind the bill at some of the actual program steps taken by the government. This government has cut official development assistance. It has cut by $56.5 million assistance to international financial institutions. The voluntary sector, NGOs, have been cut by $9.6 million; multilateral food aid, cut by $32 million; multilateral technical assistance, cut by $12.8 million; bilateral food aid, cut by $24.4 million; international humanitarian assistance, cut by $4.5 million; and geographic programs, cut by $130 million.
It is a disgrace to this Parliament; it is a disgrace to the people of this country that the government has chosen to tax the poorest in the world in an effort to deal with its own mismanagement of our financial affairs. At the same time that it is making these cuts, the government is cutting taxes to the corporate sector, cutting out a series of moves which make easier for the rich to have more and imposes these penalties on the poor in the world.
We have to change our priorities. We must see that the first on our national agenda must be those in the world who are most in need. We have opportunities in this country to provide leadership on an international scale, and it is important that we do so.
I would like to take the opportunity to refer to one particular program that this government and its predecessor has given some support to, and that is Canada World Youth. It seems to me that the government has failed to grasp in the approach that it has taken to Official Development Assistance that, by and large, the Canadian people are supportive of programs to redistribute the world's wealth and to have Canada provide leadership in international development. This is demonstrated, not only in surveys, but in the kind of commitment that Canadians have given to international development organizations; the active role that Canadians have played, for example, in organizations such as Oxfam Canada, the work that Canadians have done overseas through CUSO and CIDA.
One program in particular, I think, has provided a great base of support for a clearer understanding by Canadians of what is going on in the world. Canada World Youth was a program formed approximately 15 to 18 years ago. The inspiration for it came from Senator Jacques Hebert who used his considerable persuasive capacities to talk the Government of Canada into launching a program which has enabled thousands of young people from Canada and thousands of young people from Third World countries to work together and live together in communities both in Canada and the Third World.
Out of the experience these thousands of young people have had has come a far more realistic understanding of the reality of the world, great progress in terms of self-development for those who have participated in the program and a clearer understanding of Canada for thousands of young people in Third World countries, many of whom are already moving into positions of leadership in those countries.
Canada World Youth is a program which is funded primarily by CIDA. It is beginning to receive organizational financial assistance from other provincial governments and of course gets some funding from the private. Canada World Youth has a board of directors which is voluntary and has now an effective and experienced infrastructure to provide effective leadership in the development of the program in Canada and abroad. Each year, the program works by developing a particular protocol with a series of Third World countries and under the program young Canadians can apply to participate in a six-month program.
An equal number of young people from Third World countries are selected to participate in the program by their home countries. The young people are divided into groups, a fundamental unit of seven Canadians and seven from the exchange country. They are brought together under the standard program first to spend three months living and working in a Canadian community and that is followed by three months in a Third World community. It is for young people, generally those in the post high school age group ranging in age from 19 to 21 or 22 years, as I understand it. It has offered to young Canadians and young people from Third World countries a very distinctive experience.
October 6, 1989

I was very fortunate myself to be able to participate for a few years on the board of directors of Canada World Youth. I was actually encouraged to do that by the fact that our daughter was in the program in 1979 and spent three months in Indonesia. As a result of that, she found an interest in southeast Asia and in the Pacific which has had a major beneficial effect on her life. I know from my direct connection with other young people who participated in Canada World Youth that it is an outstanding program and one which deserves the full support of Canadians.
We live in a time when we are under great pressures, but we also live in a time when in a unique way the world is close to us. The power and impact of television brings to our homes every night the reality of what is going on in South Africa, the situation in Mozambique, the difficulties that Namibia is having as it struggles toward self-government, the tremendous problems being experienced in sub-Sahara Africa, these issues are brought daily into our lives. As a result of that, this bill has the support of the Canadian people even at a time when the government is trying to persuade the country that it is obliged to make cuts in social programs and in programs such as this one.
These issues present dramatic opportunities for Canadians to participate in terms of service and with great hope for the future. I commend this bill to the House and I urge its adoption.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Victoria on some of his remarks. I think his presence here is a reminder of the distinguished service his father gave for many years when he represented the Greenwood riding in Toronto.
Specifically I would like the member to acknowledge, if he would, that while he said many good things about Canada World Youth, surely the substance of this bill is an important step for this government to take, not only in its own right but with respect to dealing with the essential issue of the debt.
Government Orders
I have listened to a number of speakers this morning expressing concern about recent reductions in our ODA, not cuts as referred to but reductions from the targets that were originally set. Like many members I regret that those reductions have taken place. However, it is important to acknowledge that for some years now this government and its predecessors have led the way internationally in trying to take a more positive approach to the self-development that must take place in many of the countries referred to.
In particular the initiatives taken in 1986 which are now being acknowledged in this legislation with respect to the removal of some of the debt held by Canada for these sub-Saharan African countries are critically important. There is no issue that affects the developing countries of Africa more than the enormous burden of debt accumulated in the late seventies and early eighties.
By coincidence, next Friday, I will be sitting in Ethiopia having discussions on this matter with the leadership of the Economic Commission for Africa. In two weeks time we will be receiving a visit from the executive secretary of the economic commission for Africa who will meet with our Minister of Finance, with the Standing Committee on External Affairs, with the committee of finance, with voluntary groups, with African ambassadors and with those taking an active interest in Africa in order that we can have a full understanding of the important and destructive economic pressures which this massive debt has put on the people and the countries of Africa.
I think the leadership taken in this legislation is one that we should be willing to acknowledge while recognizing some of the other problems that have already been indicated.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for his kind words and the reference to my father. I know he and my father shared many perilous journeys together flying into Biafra in the dark of night with shells flying around them and even joining together to write a book which came out a few weeks late, as I recall, but still has a place on our family shelf if not the shelves of anyone else.

I am prepared to acknowledge that this bill does a little something. However, this is not even half a loaf; this is probably one slice off the far end of the loaf.
After this bill is adopted the fundamental problems still remain and remain largely untouched by the government. It has barely maintained the programs which it inherited and in fact has not provided the leadership which this area so desperately needs.
Even after this bill is passed Nigeria will have an external debt of $28 billion. This bill merely forgives loans that were interest free for a term of up to 50 years. Just think of the refugee camps in Malawi as a result of the war going on in Mozambique, over which the member and others on his side of the House including the member from Waterloo have provided leadership and assistance.
The fact remains that there is a tremendous job to do. The international financial institutions need complete restructuring so those who live in the Third World and particularly in the sub-Sahara have a real voice in the decisions made at the international economic level. We need a radical restructuring of the world's economic institutions not only for the benefit of the people in sub-Sahara Africa who are our neighbours but for our own long-term economic benefit and as a key step in the move to save the planet's environment.

speechtext: It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 35 the House will now proceed to Statements by Members under Standing Order 31.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday Premier Clyde Wells released a report on the difficulties of the fishing industry of Newfoundland and Labrador, an emerging crisis which has already been recognized by this government with the establishment of the Harris task force and a special cabinet committee.
Mr. Wells is right to be concerned about the situation. However, to propose solutions which would simply compound the burden and pass the problem to a Nova Scotian economy already facing difficulties is simply un-Canadian. What makes Canada work is our ability to achieve consensus and to share. This is how our Prime Minister was able to bring together ten premiers and the Government of Canada at Meech Lake.
If Mr. Wells wants all the fish off Newfoundland shores to remain in Newfoundland, does he also want all Ontario tax dollars to remain in Ontario and not be transferred to Newfoundlanders through equalization, regional development or UI payments?

Mr. Speaker, the RCMP has a long tradition of tolerance and understanding for the many cultures and racial groups that make up Canada. The uniform of this proud police force has evolved and changed over the years in response to new conditions. It is now appropriate that the RCMP accommodate religious groups such as Sikhs by allowing them to wear turbans as required by their faith. People of the Sikh faith should be fully represented on our national police force.
I regret greatly that members of this House are not only supporters but leaders in the attempt to prevent the modification of the RCMP dress code that would permit the entry of Sikh officers. The RCMP cannot be frozen in time. Canada is an evolving multi-ethnic community and the RCMP should fully represent this.

Mr. Speaker, dairy farmers across Canada are extremely concerned about their future. The recent GATT ruling on ice cream and yogurt threatens the very heart of the supply-management system in Canada.
In Prince Edward Island the dairy industry makes up approximately 15 per cent of the agricultural sector. There, 524 milk producers and 147 cream producers are asking questions about their future.
October 6, 1989

Across this country our farmers are wondering what is next on the chopping block as a result of this trade agreement with the United States. I urge this government to take immediate action in this crucial matter. It is essential that the dairy industry in Canada be protected.

Mr. Speaker, on September 16, over 1200 people gathered to pay tribute to the Hon. John Wise, our former minister of agriculture, for his dedication to his constituents and to the agricultural industry of Canada. John spent 16 years in this House, both as an opposition member and a minister of the Cabinet. As a member of Parliament for Elgin he ably represented the interests and concerns of his riding. As the minister of agriculture he worked to ensure that the farmers' concerns were recognized by the greater society.
I have known the former member for Elgin all my life and I can attest to his commitment to the current government's policies. It has been inferred in this House that the former member did not seek re-election because he was afraid of what might happen to supply marketing systems. This simply is not so. John Wise knew he could retire with a peaceful mind. He knew that supply-management would not be threatened by the free trade agreement. He knew Canadian farmers could and would take advantage of the challenges and opportunities afforded by this historic treaty.

Mr. Speaker, it is scandalous that the Soviet police would attack and kill innocent civilians who had gathered peacefully simply to celebrate the founding of their city of Lviv.
On October 1, citizens of that western Ukrainian city were suddenly harassed by the Soviet police. When they protested their harassment, the police viciously attacked them at the the militia headquarters leaving three dead and at least 20 people badly injured. Clearly the citizens were denied their basic human rights. As Canadians we are naturally appalled by these actions. I therefore urge the Canadian government to protest this brutal violence
against unarmed and peaceful citizens. I also ask the Canadian government to take steps to ensure that such police brutality is not repeated.
I ask the Prime Minister to take up the legitimate cause of Ukrainians in Ukraine with Mr. Gorbachev during the Prime Minister's visit scheduled to take place in the Soviet Union next month.

Mr. Speaker, on Wednesday, October 4, I attended the official opening of the Cliffwood Child Care Centre in my riding, yet another non-profit co-operative centre set up through the joint efforts of parents and the North York Board of Education.

Mr. Speaker, the Legislative Committee on Unemployment Insurance held hearings in 13 cities across Canada. It was given two hours with the minister, a day with the deputy and his staff, and one day for clause-by-clause examination of amendments to one of the most complex pieces of legislation that this House is responsible for. Yesterday we were only able to thoroughly and seriously discuss three clauses out of 57 amending clauses.

Yet the government still pulls the string.

October 6, 1989
It appears that we are trading one railroad in this country for the Tory railroading of the UI committee.

Mr. Speaker, recently in Fort Saskatchewan, the Government of Canada, along with the Government of Alberta and Sherritt Gordon, announced plans to establish the first major advanced industrial materials initiative for western Canada. The new organization, WESTAIM,is structured to assure widespread participation from universities, industries and other research organizations.
WESTAIM will be an international leader in advanced industrial materials research and development. The over-all objective of WESTAIM is to commercialize the results of applied research and development undertaken on a market-driven industry.
Advanced industrial materials are recognized as an integral part of long-term growth and diversification. The project provides the opportunity to put western Canada at the cutting edge of new technology.
Sherritt Gordon has finalized plans to move its head office from Toronto to Edmonton. The participation of the federal government in this innovative project demonstrates its strong commitment not only to research and technology but also to building a stronger economy in western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, while Canadians largely support this government's venture into space science research through the development of a Canadian space agency, there is legitimate concern that such a venture be used for non-military and peaceful purposes only.
October 6, 1989

The Minister of State has recently acknowledged that the bill to establish the space agency, Bill C-16, does not preclude its involvement in military pursuits. The auto workers' plight in and around my riding is going to get worse in the next little while because of the Mexican free enterprise zone along the U.S. border, the Maquiladora zone, which provides big business with non-unionized workers to labour in factories. These workers are paid $8 a day Canadian to work in an environment which has limited safety factors.
I would like to remind the hon. member and the House that as late as last week I received a substantial number of letters from our local merchants who reported a decrease in their sales because Canadians do their shopping across the river in the United States.
I would also like to remind him of a recent article that appeared in a Buffalo, New York newspaper which refers to their ever-booming business due to the free trade agreement and the fact that they have prospered with the Canadian businesses which have settled across the border.
The tremendous opportunities to which the hon. member has referred are for the Americans, not the Canadians.

r. Mr. Speaker, next Monday Canadians will be celebrating the traditional Thanksgiving holiday. Families and friends will be getting together to feast from this year's abundant harvest. They can give thanks that in Canada we do not suffer from production shortages and long line-ups to obtain the basic necessities of life.
Events around the world that have occurred since last Thanksgiving should cause Canadians to give extra thanks this year. A freedom rally in Tiananmen Square saw young protesters slaughtered. Even today thousands of East Germans flee their nation for a new freedom which we sometimes take for granted. Starvation and civil war in some African countries continues at an alarming rate.
Yes, Canadians have much to be grateful for and Canadians should assist those less fortunate so they can some day enjoy the same prosperity as we have. Have a happy Thanksgiving!

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this weekend most of us will have an opportunity to share with our families and friends a very important day, a day to acknowledge and be thankful for the riches we enjoy each and every day. These riches include the comfort of our families and our friends, our health, our livelihoods and this great nation we call home.
Our families are the cornerstone of our lives. They are there during the good times and the bad. They provide our strength and our vitality. We must never forget the contribution they make. It is appropriate, therefore, that Thanksgiving weekend should coincide with National Family Week.
Nor must we take for granted our country. Canada is a great nation filled with abundant resources and unlimited opportunities, a nation envied and respected by other countries of the world.

October 6, 1989
Governor General
We have a great deal to be grateful for. I want to take this opportunity to wish you, my colleagues, our staff and our families a very special Thanksgiving Day.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I rise to inform the House that Her Majesty the Queen has graciously approved the appointment, upon my recommendation, of the Hon. Raymon Hnatyshyn as the next Governor General of Canada.
Hear, hear!
The installation will take place early in the new year and those who joined in the standing ovation will be invited. There will be a special levee for the rest of you.
Hear, hear!

Hon. members need no introduction to Mr. Hnatyshyn who served in this House for over 14 years and as a Minister of the Crown for over five. Born in Saskatoon, Mr. Hnatyshyn is the son of a distinguished senator who himself was a symbol of the courage that developed the great heartland of western Canada. Both Mr. Hnatyshyn and his wife Gerda are representative of the cultural strength and diversity of Canada; he, born of proud Ukrainian stock and she, the daughter of Danish immigrants.
Mr. Hnatyshyn is known to all Canadians as a man of great warmth, civility and personal integrity.

Mr. Hnatyshyn, who was first elected as a member of this House in 1974, studied at the University of Saskatchewan and, after becoming a lawyer, was appointed Queen's Counsel in 1973.
This House will also recall his distinguished career as Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in 1979, then later as Government House Leader and Chairman of the Privy Council before becoming Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada.

As leader of the government in the House of Commons, Mr. Hnatyshyn clearly earned the respect and
trust of all members of this House. He has, I think, truly been one of the effective parliamentarians of his time and one known to all members of this House as a gentleman who conducted himself with genuine courtesy toward others and good humour in his dealings with us all.

During the debate on official languages, our former colleague, the architect of the bill, reaffirmed his personnel commitment to both official languages, and I quote:
"This Bill reflects the open-mindedness and tolerance of
Canadians in matters of language and culture. This generosity of
Canadians toward each is one of the most endearing features of our
national identity."
In recommending passage of the bill, he added:
This Bill is about fairness. This Bill is about equity of treatment of
our fellow Canadians. This Bill is about the way in which we treat. ..
Of course, as Minister of Justice, Mr. Hnatyshyn played a key role in the Meech Lake Accord negotiations which seeks to bring back the province of Quebec into the Canadian constitutional family.
Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary to remind members of both the constitutional and symbolic importance of the position of Governor General.
In recommending this appointment to Her Majesty, I was conscious of the personal dignity, the vast experience and the profound understanding of this nation and its institutions that is required of all those chosen to hold this high office. I know members from all comers of this chamber and all political parties will agree that Mr. Hnatyshyn will more than meet the expectations of Canadians in this regard.
He will bring to this vital institution, I think, a generous vision and an impressive dedication that will complement that of his distinguished predecessors, all of whom have served Canada so well.

I also take this opportunity to pay tribute, on behalf of all Canadians, to Jeanne Sauve and her husband Maurice who performed their role with great distinction and dignity and whom we shall always remember very warmly-
October 6, 1989
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues, I wish to extend our congratulations and best wishes to Ray Hnatyshyn on his appointment to the position of Governor General of Canada.

Ray Hnatyshyn is a respected scholar, lawyer and parliamentarian. He is a man who has worked his way to the top in all of his callings. To a lawyer, what greater honour can come than to be Attorney General of Canada; to a parliamentarian, what greater task is there than that of the leader of the government in the House of Commons; to a Canadian patriot and statesman, what greater distinction could come than to be called upon to serve as Governor General?
Canadians of Ukrainian origin, and all Canadians in fact, will be especially pleased with Mr. Hnatyshyn's appointment. He grew up steeped in his cultural heritage and he has always been a proud and effective example of what that community has contributed to Canada. But above all, Ray Hnatyshyn has been a proud Canadian.

Mr. Speaker, those of us who worked with Mr. Hnatyshyn know him as a warm and generous man who is very committed to the cause of human dignity.
We believe that he and his family will be worthy successors to Mrs. Sauve and her family, whom we also wish, at this opportunity, to congratulate and thank for their excellent work.

Once again, our congratulations and best wishes to Ray Hnatyshyn.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of my colleagues, I rise to compliment the Government of Canada and the Prime Minister on an extremely wise selection and recommendation of the Hon. Ray Hnatyshyn as our next Governor General.

Hear, hear!
Mr. Broadbent I say to the Prime Minister, Your Honour, in passing, he observed that those who were
Governor General
standing at the time of his announcement would be invited to the inaugural dinner, and I want to assure him that those of us who were not standing at that time in my section of the House were not in any way doing so out of the slightest disagreement. We were discussing Question Period strategy at the time as the Prime Minister, I think, will well understand. We look forward, therefore, to being invited to that dinner.

Hear, hear!
The man who is about to assume this extremely important position in our parliamentary democracy has served his country well in his home province of Saskatchewan and beyond. He has been a minister of the Crown holding a number of important responsibilities; Minister of Energy, Minister of State for Science and Technology, government House leader, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Justice.
His government House leader experience ought to have normally been sufficient to annoy all members on this side of the House but, quite to the contrary, he handled that in a tough-minded way, as he is supposed to, but with a congeniality and affability of manner that earned warm respect, if at times partisan antagonism, from this side of the House.
He has, as has already been indicated, Your Honour, always had a broad view of this country. He grew up on the prairies but, like politicians of all parties who in one sense, if I can put it this way, rise to the occasion, he developed a broad sense of what Canada is all about without losing in the slightest his own deep commitment to the region in which he grew up.

Mr. Speaker, Ray Hnatyshyn is a western Canadian whose ancestors are neither French nor English; that is, he represents an important dimension of our people. Mr. Hnatyshyn has a warm personality, a desirable quality for a Governor General.

His openness and his warmth will bring a human touch to a dignified position. We wish him well.

Hear, hear!

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment. Yesterday the minister was booed in Quebec. His proposal to invite young Canadians to Canada's parks to discuss the environment is utterly hypocritical. Young people know very well that the Conservative policy on the environment is a fraud. Why does the minister claim that the environment is his priority when the cuts to VIA Rail were made without regard to environmental considerations?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Hamilton East should go to Quebec from time to time to realize that Quebecers are very polite, very courteous and very eager to talk about the environment. Member to check with those who were there to see that we had an extremely interesting discussion which is veiy promising for the future. Mr. Speaker, the Minister is very good at making promises, but he does not deliver the goods; he did not deliver on VIA Rail.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader; Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: Which will cost dearly, besides.

My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.

During the election the Prime Minister stated in Hamilton, and I quote:
In considering any development, any project and any program, we will make its environmental consequences as fundamental a test as we now apply to its economic feasibility.
Why did he say that when the VIA cuts show clearly he did not mean it? Why did the Prime Minister say yes to VIA cuts and no to the environment?

Mr. Speaker, I told the Hon. Member for Hamilton East several times that we have environmental legislation, that in general the Conservative Government respects the law, and that as part of the process to set up a new VIA Rail network, we conducted the necessary preliminary studies to determine the environmental impact of the new route network. Transport Department officials, in cooperation with those from the Environment Department, came to the conclusion that the environmental impact of the new network would be negligible and for that reason, it was not necessary to pursue environmental studies further. I even said that we would produce a document confirming these statements in the coming days.
So I ask the hon. member, instead of playing politics with the environment, to respect the law and look at the relevant documents which will prove to her that we did what we had to do.
My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. I expect an answer-
Oh, oh!

-because it was the Prime Minister who made all the promises about the environment.
The government's own cabinet document, which I assume the Prime Minister has read, states quite clearly that the decision to cut VIA will result in an increase in car travel, and an increase in the burning of fossil fuels. That cut in VIA will mean more acid rain and greater greenhouse effects.
On the eve of the American decision to cut acid rain, why is the Prime Minister approving the cut in VIA Rail which will actually result in an increase in acid rain in Canada and an increase in greenhouse gases? How can he do that with a straight face?

Mr. Speaker, this is a misrepresentation of the facts. The facts are quite clear. The environmental impact of this decision will be negligible.
October 6, 1989

The study conducted in Transport Canada has been reviewed by my officials. They completely and strongly agree with the conclusions drawn by the Transport Canada authorities.
There is no way that Canadians will believe that this decision is bad for the environment. Actually, it is very good for the environment because it will provide Canada with a way to devote more money to environment and to wipe out the deficit.
There is no way that Canadians will believe that it is better for the environment to go around the country with empty trains instead of putting people in buses. Experiments on buses have demonstrated that they are much more environmentally sound than trains.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. First of all, I want to tell the Minister of the Environment that there are no empty trains in the west.
One hundred and ten years ago Canadians built the train service from Toronto to Calgary so they could travel through Canada. They were tired of taking ox carts from the states. We have right now taken a giant step backward. If you want to take a train from Toronto to Calgary, you have to go through Chicago, Minneapolis, Minot, Grand Forks, and to Montana and then three days later you get on a bus and go to Calgary.
Given that we are actually financing the Amtrak expansion, does the Minister think we have to provide them with the passengers too?

Mr. Speaker, my friend is from Manitoba in western Canada. I would like to give the member some ridership occupancy rates in Manitoba. For Wabowden-Churchill it is 7 per cent. We have Winnipeg-Capreol at 22 per cent.

speechtext: Capreol is in Ontario, not western Canada.

I would be delighted to say that there is no occupancy rate over 60 per cent except one, which is the Transcontinental, and we consider everybody who stops at every station.
The decision is very sound. It corresponds with what Canadians want. They want a national network. We have a national network.

Canadians know that this country has to live with affordable expenditures. Increasingly, Canadians are accepting that we manage the country with a network that, once again, is national, sustainable, and affordable. You will increasingly be seeing this government use good management of money for Canadians.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, as the minister knows, Winnipeg is in Manitoba but Capreol is a thousand miles away in northern Ontario.
My supplementary question is for the Prime Minister. When a deal was struck between Canada and British Columbia in 1871 the federal government agreed in the Constitution to provide and maintain rail services to and within British Columbia. The people of British Columbia want to know if there is no constitutional guarantee for rail passenger services exactly what this guarantee means in the Constitution.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of the Environment who had the nerve to get up and say that this decision about VIA would have a net positive impact on the environment.

We have waited for 48 hours. Where is the study?
October 6, 1989

I said Wednesday, Mr. Speaker, and I repeat today that this document will be available in the coming days. The coming days could be today, Monday or Tuesday. But the member has nothing to be worried about. He will get the study and then he will see that we were right.

Mr. Speaker, we all know that the minister and his officials are going to have a busy weekend.
We checked with VIA this morning. It may be of interest for the minister to know that VIA officials said this morning that they know nothing about such a study. They did not participate in such a study. In fact, they said that the only thing they know about is what the minister said in the House.
I want to ask the minister how the people of Canada can take seriously a claim that environmental considerations were seriously undertaken when the people directly involved, namely, VIA Rail, said they weren't even consulted on it.

Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the NDP should know that VIA Rail is a corporation, it is not a person. In the government it is a person-the Minister of Transport-who is responsible for the preliminary study. I am the Minister of Transport. I did the study. I concluded that we do not need any other studies.

Mr. Speaker, it is truly amazing that the minister did the study locked away in his closet and did not consult VIA Rail, the people presumably who know something about laying down tracks, cars, and so on. They were not consulted, and the minister says that he did the study. God protect us! That's all I can say if he did it on his own.

But if the Minister did that wonderful study, where is it? He said that he did the study. Why is it not here for Hon. Members to look at before the weekend? The study is done. Where is it?

Mr. Speaker, I just said, and I repeat, that the study will be produced in the coming days and that it will prove we were right. That being said,
I also stated just now that the Minister is responsible for
making the decision. That is what we did. I did not say that we did not consult or that officials of any level within VIA Rail were not given an opportunity to give their opinions-that is very obvious-in cooperation with the officials of my colleague in the Environment Department. The decision was made by the Minister of Transport. The documents will be produced and, again, the Leader of the New Democratic Party will rest easy because he will realize that the studies were well done and obviously came to the conclusion that I told him before.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of State for Transport, who just last week said she would not comment on leaked documents concerning VIA Rail, my question is to the Minister of Transport.
According to a government document-and we are speaking of studies here-"Canadians already are confronted with airport and highway congestion, particularly at Pearson International Airport and on the highways around Toronto and in southwestern Ontario. Population and travel growth will result in even greater congestion".
How can the Minister of Transport support cuts to VIA Rail-in the Hamilton-Toronto-Niagara route alone of one-third, not to mention the rest of southwestern Ontario-which will result in even further congestion on already clogged highways in southern and southwestern Ontario? How can he support these cuts?

Very simply, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that you will understand if I tell you, first, I do not know about the document because it has not been tabled. But the occupancy rate between Toronto and Niagara Falls is 46 per cent. We did not stop the train between Niagara Falls and Toronto. We maintained the train. But if the occupancy rate is at 70 to 75 per cent, we will serve the same number of people. It is mathematically understandable.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Travellers to the nation's capital, both business and tourist, are faced with dreadful road networks and poor air service. They often have chosen to come to the nation's capital by rail.
October 6, 1989

Ottawa will be severely disadvantaged through the axing of The Canadian and the reduction of the Mon-treal-Ottawa route from five to two runs. There will be no rail service in Ottawa after 5 p.m.
Why would the Prime Minister of Canada again savage the capital of this nation?

Mr. Speaker, I am very surprised because Ottawa is probably one of the best served cities in Canada in terms of rail. I am sure that many people who hear what you are saying today will be very surprised.
Once again, the same argument as for my friend from Hamilton applies. For example, the occupancy rate between Toronto and Ottawa is about 50 per cent. If we increase the occupancy rate I believe we will do two very important things. We will serve Canadians from Ottawa to Toronto, and we will save money. I think Canadians increasingly will understand that we have this national network, which you said so many times that we should keep. It is there. But, once again, I think my friend understands in the bottom of his heart that we have to protect the finances of this country, too. He knows very well that he lives in a region where there are many other modes of transportation for citizens.
To permit all Canadians from Halifax to Vancouver to have different modes of transportation, but particularly

the train where people do not have any other mode of transportation, is the basis of the decision that we made. Canadians want a transportation system that is the best, affordable, but also the most accessible for all Canadians.

Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External
Affairs): Mr. Speaker, I can assure the hon. member and members of the House that the Government of Canada is not considering any move away from the traditional shares of the stock between Newfoundland and Nova Scotia.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance. The Toronto-Dominion Bank agrees that this government's fiscal and monetary policies are driving Canada towards recession. When is this government going to wake up?
Mr. Speaker, obviously the hon. member has not been paying attention. Rates were up one percentage point in most European countries yesterday. In Canada, they did not move at all.

Mr. Speaker, our short-term interest rates in Canada are 4.47 percentage points higher than in the United States. up sales and excise taxes in its last budget by more than $3 billion. It is a government that is now going to saddle us with a goods and services tax. These are the things that cause inflation.
When is this government going to accept its responsibility and wake up to the new world realities? Our interest rates are dramatically out of line and they themselves are a major cause of inflation and government expense. Every percentage point rise in the interest rate increases our deficit by $1.6 billion. This is not strong fiscal management.

Mr. Speaker, let me be quite clear with hon. members. What is causing inflation is a range of things, including the fact that the economy has been growing more quickly than the capacity of the country to handle that growth.
Oh, oh!

All across the country you are a joke.

In a sense I think that I have made the point that, on balance, we have no concern with the role and the effectiveness of the chairs of standing committees. They do an excellent job under difficult circumstances.
However, there are some where we have difficulties. There have been some committees that have refused to meet. The energy committee was one of those committees. At a time when a number of energy crises were before the country, the chair refused to call the committee together. We have had difficulties from time to time.
I am focusing on one individual. I must say I personally find it difficult to do that, because in terms of his knowledge of financial matters, and the leadership that he has given the finance committee, and the status to which he has elevated the finance committee to deal with complicated matters he has been exemplary. But, unfortunately, I cannot, as a parliamentarian, simply stand by when a chair of a committee who I believe represents the members of that committee, makes such inappropriate and unacceptable statements regarding Canadian citizens. It is for that reason I have intervened in this process where normally an intervention would never be necessary.
Having registered concerns on behalf of the New Democratic Party, we will pass this motion on division. The intention, of course, is to register our concerns with the words uttered by the chair as a reflection against upstanding Canadian citizens from all parts of the country.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words on behalf of what I hope is the entire striking committee which has representation from all three parties in the House.
The job of recommending to the House the members of committees is not the easiest job in the world and from time to time there is some discord in the House. But I believe members of the striking committee are rather consistently guided in their attempts to choose members to be on our standing committees and from time to time on our legislative committees who will work hard, do the job, and who bring to that job some considerable background and expertise. Members of the striking committee are concerned about the quality of the research, the quality of the advice, and the quality of the reports that come back for consideration by all members of the House.
From time to time it is unfortunate when members of the House use an inadvertent set of words or a deliberate set of words that are perhaps inflammatory. Those of us who have been around for ten years or longer have sometimes seen an awakening of public understanding of something that comes from those attempts. Sometimes we should not be as hasty as we might be to condemn a particular set of words, because there is a message in them. Sometimes in this House the words we use are so flowery and so complex that they defy understanding by most Canadians. Sometimes, I wonder if even those who utter the words really comprehend what they have just said.

October 6, 1989
Routine Proceedings
Any quarrel that the House leader of the New Democratic Party has with the member is appropriately taken up when the member is present. It is perhaps unfortunate that the debate arose at this time. We have had through the process of parliamentary reform in the last five years a great deal of co-operation in evolving and developing the methods that help parliamentarians to participate in a much fuller way in the development of public policy. The particular exercise that took place in Edmonton this week with the finance committee travelling was not the kind of common exercise that existed in this place when I first came 10 years ago.
What is before the finance committee at this point is a proposal, a technical paper. Members of that committee, members from all sides of the House have been asked to go out, hear the Canadian people, come back to the House with advice as to whether the content of that technical paper will help Canadians.
Members of committees who travel experience a sense of frustration from time to time because people come with complaints without having done the background work that would indicate to the members of the committee that they have read the document and therefore are speaking to the document. It is my understanding that that has happened more than once in the finance committee's hearings in different places. It certainly was happening with the committee on unemployment insurance as it travelled the country.
When members are travelling and moving from community to community, day to day and working from early in the morning until late at night on our behalf, they get a little short tempered sometimes; they may become a little less prudent than they might be. All of us can take comfort in the reality that the finance committee, including its chairman, is one of the hardest working committees in this House. This has been true for several years now. It is one of the best informed committees of this House. When you look back at the end of the year they will have held more meetings than perhaps any other committee of this House. The quality of the work that they do is not always accepted by everybody, but
there is nobody who can make the statement that the finance committee does not do a lot of homework and produce a sensible set of ideas as a consequence of understanding what it is that they are about. When that happens with a committee I think the chairman must receive some of the credit at least.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to bring the motion into context, the purpose of the motion and the reason why we gave our consent to it was to simplify matters. Members will know that Standing Order 106 states:
Within ten sitting days following the adoption by the House of a report of the Striking Committee, the Clerk of the House shall convene a meeting of each standing committee whose membership is contained in that report for the purpose of electing a Chairman, provided that forty-eight hours' notice is given of any such meeting.
The reason why we put this motion is in the interest of all committees so they can keep operating without having to go through the rigmarole of elections again. It is quite clear that the second part of the motion states: "Provided that those Standing and/or Standing Join Committees whose chairmen cease to be members of the committee shall proceed to the election of a new chairman as their first order of business." The purpose is to help committees continue with their work, and personally I think they are doing an awful lot of good work without having to go through the election in every committee of a chair and a vice-chair. Basically, we gave our support to that. We will enter into any debate as to whether members of certain committees are not holding meetings regularly or whether there are chairmen of committee or chairpersons of committees making remarks that we do not agree with, we will use committees to do that, not the House.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mrs. Landry that Bill C-10, an act relating to the forgiveness of debts incurred or assumed in respect of certain official development assistance loans made by the Government of Canada to the governments of certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa, be read the third time and passed.

Mr. Speaker, I feel very privileged to stand here in the House and speak very briefly to Bill C-10, an act relating to the forgiveness of debts incurred or assumed in respect of certain official development assistance loans made by the Government of Canada to the governments of certain countries in sub-Saharan Africa.

October 6, 1989
Government Orders
The government certainly should be commended for forgiving these debts. However, I think that we are overlooking something that has a much greater implication for the people of the sub-Saharan Africa than the forgiveness of debts. It is the human need, the human suffering, and the economic need that is present in the Third World countries today.
Canada has a decade of achievement on humanitarian grounds, on the approach that we have taken to people in need, but this accomplishment is being threatened for almost 900 million people; in other words one-sixth of mankind is sliding backward into poverty. That is a dreadful situation. We are all very concerned about our own debt here in Canada today. Some people applaud this government and the fact that it has cut back in foreign aid to the Third World countries.
I do not know how we can consider the steps the government has taken as brave when we look at the poverty and the children who are dying around the world. Of course we are concerned about our own, but we cannot be so narrow as to look only at our own nation. We have to look beyond our boundaries.
This government has reduced its commitment to Third World development and to the world poor. We know the bill has no impact on the budget of our country. Although the bill forgives debt, the government has not taken the leadership that has consistently been shown by Canada for a great number of years. Canada now ranks last among middle income developed countries as to its level of ODA. I do not think that is something we should all be very proud of as a nation.
It is a tragic situation when 40,000 children are dying every day in this world from malnutrition. The State of the World's Children 1989 states that it is the young child whose growing mind and body are susceptible to permanent damage from even temporary deprivation. It is the young child whose individual development today and whose social contribution tomorrow are being shaped by the economics of now. It is the young child who is paying the highest of all prices and who will bear the most recurring of all costs for the mounting debt repayments, the drop in export earnings, the increase in food costs,
the fall in family incomes, the run down of health services, and the narrowing of educational opportunities.
It is simply no longer necessary for approximately
40,000	young children to die every day in developing worlds and for so many millions more to live on with ill health and poor growth. Today the world is both aware that this tragedy is happening and capable of preventing it and ethics must march with awareness, morality with capacity. It is the poor and the vulnerable who are suffering the most and for two main reasons: the first is that the poor have the least economic fat with which to absorb the blow of recession. The second reason is that the poor also have the least political muscle to ward off that blow. The Government of Canada is not responding as it originally promised. It is an irresponsible attitude to a major world problem. I support the bill but I beseech the government to address the serious problems of the world's hunger and economic ills. Of course we must relate to our own debt as well as to the world debt. We cannot work in the isolation of what is happening in our own country. We all must become self-reliant. The government has taken the right step to introduce a bill to forgive the debt but takes no leadership in dealing with the root causes of poverty and debt.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a very short comment on debate.
I believe this is an important albeit rather insignificant piece of legislation. We applaud this initiative called Bill C-10, which is really a bill to write off debts that the Government of Canada has made with a number of governments of African countries, namely the Republic of the Cameroon, the People's Republic of the Congo, Republic of the Ivory Coast, the Gabonese Republic, the Republic of Ghana, the Republic of Kenya, the Democratic Republic of Madagascar, the Federal Republic of Nigeria, the Republic of Senegal, Republic of Swaziland, Republic of Zaire, Republic of Zambia, and Republic of Zimbabwe.
This bill is a small step in the right direction and for that we are thankful, but it will go no way toward eliminating the horrendous debts faced by these countries. I draw to the House's attention that after this bill is passed Nigeria will still find itself with a debt in excess of $28 billion, Kenya with a debt in excess of $6 billion, and so on. These are countries where the situation is almost impossible under these oppressive debt loads, but the Government of Canada has taken this small step and for that I applaud it.
October 6, 1989

I want to make two short points. We do not want to leave the impression that the government is actually serious about foreign assistance. Not long ago the Prime Minister made a commitment on behalf of the Government of Canada when he spoke before the United Nations that it was Canada's intention to achieve a Overseas Development Assistance package relative to GNP with a ratio of 0.7 per cent by the year 2000. Mr. Speaker, 0.7 per cent of GNP going into Overseas Development Assistance would be an acceptable level and has been agreed for many years to be an acceptable level. Recently the government announced we will not reach that level of 0.7 per cent of GNP until at least the year 2040, so we have seen a reneging on that kind of commitment.
We only have to look at the last budget to be reminded of the cuts that have taken place: for international financial institutions, a cut of $56.5 million; for the voluntary sector, the non-governmental organizations, their budget was cut by $9.6 million. Multilateral food aid was cut by $32 million; multilateral technical assistance, cut by $12.8 million; bilateral food aid, cut by $24.4 million; international humanitarian assistance aid, cut by $4.5 million; geographic programs, cut by $130 million.
Mr. Speaker, here is the actual evidence. The proof, if you like, is in the eating of the pudding and when you eat it you find out that the government has substantially reduced in all areas its commitment to assisting those in need in the developing nations. Finally I am concerned with the comments made recently by the Minister of Finance when he was speaking at the Commonwealth Finance Ministers' Meeting in Kingston, Jamaica, on September 20, 1989, when he said: "Without the implementation of sustainable adjustment policies that lead to the re-establishment of self-sustaining growth, debt reduction and debt relief-" and I stress this point-"that debt reduction and debt relief do little more than buy time. Better domestic policies, not debt relief, are the key to sustained growth".
I become very concerned with those kinds of comments. Is this an indication that in terms of programs and action of debt relief the government is not interested in
Government Orders
pursuing those options. By the fact that we have these overwhelming debt albatrosses around the necks of the developing countries, particularly the very poorest, is this government indicating that really what it needs is better domestic policies?
Let us be reminded that the prosperity that those of us in the first world countries and second world countries have was built originally by the exploitation of those third and fourth world countries. Therein lie the problems that they have today. The fundamental problem that they face in developing their domestic economic policies is the fact that we, as developed countries, exploited them so ruthlessly for so many years. They are really starting far back in the development process as a result of that exploitation.
We have an obligation as a country along with other western nations particularly to do what we can. While we applaud this small step in this minute debt forgiveness in terms of government to government loans, this only is the beginning and we will be pressing for a host of other initiatives that we hopefully will see taken soon.
